idiom_name: one hub object + a narrow notify/emit interface + colleagues holding only that interface
implementation_notes: Language-neutral form: give the collaboration a single hub that declares one narrow notification entry point (notify(sender, event) or a typed emit), let every participant hold a reference to the hub abstraction and route outgoing interactions through it, and keep the coordination rules inside the hub's implementation. Colleagues must never see each other's concrete types; the hub may know them. Registration must be symmetric (subscribe/unsubscribe) and lifetime-aware, because the hub is usually the longest-lived object and a strong listener registry turns it into a leak. Prefer a typed event vocabulary over stringly-typed payloads, and decide explicitly whether dispatch is synchronous and whether handlers may re-enter the hub. Modern implementations use sealed/class hierarchies (Java sealed interfaces, C# discriminated unions, TypeScript discriminated unions, Python dataclasses/Enum) to get compiler-verified exhaustiveness on event handlers.
code_sketch:
hub = Mediator()
hub.register(colleague_a); hub.register(colleague_b)
# a colleague reports; the hub decides who reacts
hub.notify(sender=colleague_a, event=Check(checked=True))
pitfalls: Letting the hub absorb the colleagues' domain logic until it becomes a god object and the participants are anemic data holders.
Asymmetric registration: colleagues subscribe but are never removed, so the hub keeps dead participants alive.
Untyped event strings and payloads: typos create listeners that never fire and no compiler complains.
Dispatch that re-enters the hub (a handler triggering another notification) without an explicit re-entrancy rule.
Typed event proliferation: each new interaction adds a new event type to the mediator's interface, growing the public surface until it is as tightly coupled as the original direct-calling code.
Missing failure semantics: undefined retry policy, timeout budget, or compensation behaviour when a colleague is unreachable.

Assuming an in-process mediator supplies transport durability: it does not provide cross-process delivery or recovery after process failure, so durable messaging or workflow infrastructure is required when those guarantees matter.
